label: Institution
name: Al Rashid
summary:
The Al-Rashid dynasty of Ha'il (Emirate of Jabal Shammar), founded 1836 by Abdullah ibn Rashid in the Najd region of central Arabia, was the main rival to the Al-Saud dynasty in the 19th and early 20th centuries — capturing Riyadh and expelling the Al-Saud in 1891, ruling most of northern and central Arabia for decades, and finally being absorbed by Ibn Saud's reconquering Al-Saud when the Emirate of Ha'il fell to Saudi forces in 1921. The Al-Rashid briefly appeared to be the dynasty that would unite the Arabian Peninsula.

Abdullah ibn Rashid established the Emirate of Jabal Shammar in the 1830s as a client of the Egyptian Muhammad Ali's expanding influence in Arabia, then achieved independence. His successors — particularly Muhammad ibn Rashid (r. 1869-1897, the 'Lion of the Najd') — expanded the emirate to its peak: capturing Riyadh (1891), expelling the Al-Saud, and controlling territory from the Hejaz border to the Persian Gulf coast. Muhammad ibn Rashid is considered one of the greatest Arab military commanders of the 19th century.

The emirate's decline resulted from repeated succession crises (multiple amirs assassinated by relatives) and the resurgent Al-Saud under Ibn Saud (Abdulaziz ibn Saud), who captured Riyadh in 1902 with 40 men and systematically reconquered Najd. Ha'il fell in 1921 after a siege; the last Amir Saud ibn Rashid surrendered. The Al-Rashid family was relocated to Riyadh under house arrest (later integrated into Saudi elite). The rivalry is a foundational narrative of modern Saudi state-formation.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Al-Rashid dynasty of Ha'il — briefly capturing Riyadh and controlling most of Arabia — reminds that the Saudi state's eventual dominance was contingent: the Arabian Peninsula might have been unified under the Rashidis instead, with profound consequences for 20th-century Islam and oil history.
